judgments.reasoning_cat1: 'Sections 10.3 through 10.5' is a clean range and 'court of competent jurisdiction' is a term of art. The only softness is that the phrase is left undefined by the compact itself.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: New York § 634 defines 'court of competent jurisdiction' differently for this very section (an Article 78 court) than for the compact generally, and 15.1(p) grants original federal district-court jurisdiction over all cases arising under the compact. Three provisions describe the reviewing forum, which invites argument.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: 'Each state shall provide for the maintenance and preservation of such records... as the commission shall prescribe' is a definite duty with content delegated to the commission. Little to construe.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: It obliges 'each state' although 1.2(h) makes the federal government a 'signatory party' but not a 'state', so the federal government is silently excluded; consistent with 15.1's general federal reservations. Minor.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: 'Whenever the commission finds it necessary or desirable to exercise the powers conferred by this article' is self-judging, and 'superseded to the extent of any conflict' leaves the boundary of supersession to be worked out case by case. Both nameable.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: It supersedes exactly the state permits that 10.3(ii) expressly preserves, and it cuts against 1.5's preservation of existing agencies and 5.5's saving of state authority. This is a specific, identifiable clash with 10.3.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: An introductory stem stating a purpose ('avoiding conflicts of jurisdiction') and making the rules 'subject in each case to the provisions of Section 1.4'. The stem itself is clear.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: Making federal project rules 'subject to' Section 1.4's reservation of congressional powers means the rules yield wherever Congress's navigation or commerce powers are engaged, which substantially undercuts (b); and 15.1(s) adds yet another layer of qualification. The stem is where those tensions are anchored.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: 'All projects related to powers delegated to the commission' uses the elastic 'related to' and gives no content to 'consultation'. Modest but nameable.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: It applies to federal projects but is subject to 1.4 and to 15.1(s), which subordinates the whole scheme to federal constitutional authority and lets the President delete plan provisions. The consultation duty survives, but its bite is uncertain.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: 'No expenditure or commitment shall be made... nor shall it be deemed authorized, unless it shall have first been included by the commission in the comprehensive plan' is a flat bar, but 'nor shall it be deemed authorized' purports to unauthorise congressionally authorised federal projects — a striking reach whose meaning is contestable. The added clause distinguishes it from 11.2(b) for no stated reason.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: It conditions all federal spending on plan inclusion while 1.4 reserves congressional power, 15.1(a) requires congressional authorisation of commission projects, and 15.1(s) allows the President to delete plan provisions and requires only that federal action 'not substantially conflict' with the plan. Those provisions cannot all be given literal effect together.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: A saving clause preserving existing federal agency authority 'except as specifically provided by this section'. Clear on its face.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: It preserves federal agency authority in the same breath that (b) makes any expenditure unauthorised absent plan inclusion — the saving and the bar sit in the same three-paragraph section pointing opposite ways. That is a nameable internal inconsistency.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: An introductory stem parallel to 11.1 but without the 'subject to Section 1.4' qualifier; the omission is deliberate and the stem is clear. Low.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: It governs state and local projects while 1.5 preserves existing state agencies and 10.8 supersedes state permits — overlapping regimes, but the stem itself does not create the clash. Moderate-low.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: Word-for-word the same as 11.1(a), with the same elastic 'related to' and undefined 'consultation'. Modest.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: Duplicates 11.1(a) for state projects; consistent within the article. Low-moderate.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: 'No expenditure or commitment shall be made... unless it shall have first been included by the commission in the comprehensive plan' is a sweeping prohibition on state and local spending with no de minimis threshold and no exception. Its literal breadth is its problem.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: Section 3.8 conditions projects on 'substantial effect' and approval, whereas this paragraph conditions all state and local project spending on prior plan inclusion — two different gates for the same activity — and 11.2(c) then preserves state agency authority. Harmonising the three is a genuine construction problem.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: A saving clause for state and local agency authority 'except as specifically provided by this section'. Clear.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: It preserves state authority alongside (b)'s bar on any expenditure not in the plan, and alongside 10.8's supersession and New York § 641's disapplication of inconsistent state law. The saving and the bar pull against each other within one section.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: A reservation of state taxing power measured by withdrawal or diversion, limited to use 'within the jurisdictions of the respective signatory parties'. Concrete.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: It reserves state charges on the same withdrawals that 3.5(b) forbids the commission to charge, that 4.3 lets the commission assess, and that 15.1(b) protects from charge altogether — and 14.3 exempts the commission itself from state taxation. Several charge regimes overlap on one subject.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: 'Uniform standards and procedures' and 'equitable cost sharing and reimbursement formulas' are broad but are directives to create rules rather than rules themselves. Modest.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: It anchors 12.20(a)'s cost-sharing plan and 13.3's apportionment, and 15.1(a) requires congressional review of cost apportionment for federal projects. Coordinated.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: 'Uniform and consistent procedures for the allocation of project costs' — abstract but not ambiguous in any operative way. Low.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: Uses 'cost' as defined in 1.2(d), which includes the vague 'net induced adverse effects'; that imported vagueness is the only real interaction. Low.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: A list of arrangements to be developed; nothing to construe.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: Feeds 12.20(a) and 14.13; consistent. Low.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: An accounting-system directive; concrete and administrative. Low.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: Coheres with 14.11's audit provisions and 13.3's budget machinery. Low.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: 'Payments in lieu of taxes' is defined operationally in 14.3, not here, and 'determining the basis and apportioning amounts' is left open. Modest.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: Section 14.3 already fixes the in-lieu payment formula (equal to taxes for the year before acquisition, for ten years), so this paragraph's grant of discretion to apportion in-lieu payments overlaps a prescribed formula. A small but real doubling.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: Two obligations in one sentence — the commission 'shall furnish' services, each party 'pledges itself to provide' services 'within the limits of available appropriations' — with the appropriations proviso arguably attaching to both. The final 'may be reimbursable whenever the parties deem appropriate' leaves cost allocation wholly open.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: Section 15.1(h) expressly overrides this section for the United States, reducing the federal pledge to whatever agencies agree or the President directs, and New York § 638 restates the state pledge; so the mutual pledge is asymmetric in practice. The override is drafted deliberately.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: The section says bonds are 'payable solely out of the properties and revenues of the commission without recourse to taxation' and in the next breath that they are 'direct and general obligations of the commission' with 'the full faith and credit of the commission' pledged — those two characterisations sit uneasily together and a bondholder and the commission would read them differently. That internal juxtaposition is a nameable ambiguity.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: Read with 12.3 (no power to pledge any signatory's credit) and 12.18 (a first and exclusive lien on identified revenues), the 'full faith and credit' pledge has no clear content beyond the commission's own assets. The three provisions must be harmonised.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: The opening — 'The purpose of this compact shall include without limitation thereto all costs of any project' — is a mechanical oddity: a section headed 'Funds and Expenses' that redefines 'the purpose of this compact' as a list of costs. Read literally it is close to nonsense and plainly means 'purposes for which bonds may be issued'.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: The phrase 'purposes of this compact' recurs throughout (1.5, 3.6(a), 12.1, 14.1), so a provision purporting to enlarge that phrase to cover bond issuance costs has instrument-wide reach it cannot have been meant to have. That mismatch is genuine.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: A flat exclusion of signatory and municipal credit plus a personal-immunity sentence; both are definite. Low.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: Section 12.20(b) permits bonds to be sold 'with or without the guaranty of such signatory party', which is in tension with the flat statement that the commission may not 'impose any obligation for payment of the bonds upon any signatory party'. The guaranty is voluntary, which mostly reconciles them.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: A detailed refunding power; 'duplicate interest' is unusual but the mechanics are conventional and specific. Low.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: 'All provisions of this compact applicable to the issuance of bonds are applicable to refunding bonds' incorporates 12.7's fifty-year maturity cap and 12.13's bidding requirements, which is coherent. Low.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: Long but precise: authorisation by resolution, non-dependence of validity on proceeds or completion, series, security, denominations, redemption. Conventional bond-law drafting.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: Coheres with 12.6, 12.13 and 12.18; 12.20(b)'s 'notwithstanding any other provision' carve-out for private placement is expressly reconciled. Low.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: Very long, but the one interesting phrase — covenants 'other than any restriction on the regulatory powers vested in the commission by this compact' — draws a clear line, and the rest is a standard indenture catalogue. Low-moderate.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: The bar on covenanting away regulatory powers protects Articles 5 and 10, yet 12.18 makes pledged revenues a trust fund that cannot be used for other purposes — a mild constraint on rate-setting under 3.7 and 9.5. Reconcilable.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: 'No bond or its terms shall mature in more than fifty years from its own date' is awkwardly phrased ('or its terms' adds nothing) but the fifty-year cap and the per-bond calculation rule are numerically definite. Low.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: Consistent with 12.4's application of all issuance provisions to refunding bonds and with the compact's 100-year duration in 1.6(a). Low.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: 'Free and exempt from all taxation by or under authority of any of the signatory parties, except for transfer, inheritance and estate taxes' is definite on its face; the enumerated exceptions are closed. The trouble is not vagueness but reach.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: Section 1.2(h) makes the federal government a 'signatory party', so this exempts bonds from federal taxation — which 15.1(f) squarely denies, permitting federal exemption only to the same extent as state bonds. That is a direct, nameable conflict between two operative provisions.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: 'Bonds shall bear interest at a rate determined by the commission, payable annually or semi-annually' is short and complete as amended. Nothing to construe.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: Section 12.13 still caps net interest cost at six percent per annum on competitively sold issues, so the 1984 amendment freeing the rate leaves an unrepealed ceiling elsewhere. That is a specific residue of an amendment not carried through.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: Place and currency of payment; entirely definite. Low.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: No competing provision. Low.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: Facsimile execution and the survival of signatures after officers leave; standard and precise. Low.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: Consistent with 12.5 and 14.5. Low.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: A short power to purchase, hold, cancel or resell its own bonds 'out of any funds available therefor'. Definite.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: 'Funds available therefor' must be read against 12.18's trust-fund restriction on pledged revenues, a modest interaction. Low.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: Long and detailed, but with a real puzzle: bonds must be 'sold on sealed proposals to the highest bidder' while the operative constraint is expressed as a net interest cost cap, and the private-sale fallback is bounded by 'the lowest bid which was rejected' — highest bidder and lowest net interest cost are different measures. That mismatch is nameable.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: The six percent net-interest ceiling here survives the 1984 amendment of 12.9, which lets the commission set the rate; and 12.20(b) permits private placement 'notwithstanding any other provision', bypassing this whole regime. Two express escapes from a mandatory bidding rule.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: A one-sentence negotiability rule with a single clear exception. Low.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: Fits 12.5's authorisation of coupon or registered form. Low.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: 'Legal investments for savings banks, fiduciaries and public funds' is a closed enumeration; whether other institutional investors are covered is an expressio unius point, but a minor one. Low-moderate.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: Applies 'in each of the signatory states' but is silent as to federal fiduciaries, consistent with 15.1's federal reservations. Low.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: 'Conclusive against all persons whomsoever' is a very strong preclusive phrase, and 'in rem' validation proceedings raise questions about which forum and which law applies. Modest.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: It binds 'each of the signatory parties', including the United States, whereas 15.1(p) says nothing in the compact waives federal sovereign immunity from suit. That is a specific tension worth naming.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: A recording exemption and a pledge-perfection rule; both are technically precise. Low.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: Consistent with 12.18's lien provisions. Low.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: A very long single sentence in which the trust-fund restriction is interrupted by a lengthy 'except as and to the extent provided in the indenture' clause ending in 'or other purposes' — a catch-all that swallows the restriction it qualifies. The reference to 'all such rates, rents, tolls, fees and charges' has no clear antecedent within the section.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: The exclusive lien here must be reconciled with 12.6's bar on covenants restricting regulatory powers and with 3.7 and 9.5's rate-setting standards, and the antecedent for 'such rates' is really 3.7 and 12.6. The missing antecedent is a genuine drafting relationship problem.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: Enumerated remedies followed by an express non-exclusivity sentence, which forecloses the usual expressio unius argument. Well drafted for its purpose.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: 'A court of competent jurisdiction of any signatory party' interacts with 15.1(p)'s federal jurisdiction grant and immunity reservation, and with New York § 634. Overlapping forums but no contradiction.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: 'The signatory parties will provide such capital funds... as may be authorized by their respective statutes' followed by 'nothing in this section shall be deemed to impose any mandatory obligation' — the covenant is negated by its own proviso, leaving it unclear whether anything was promised. That self-cancelling structure is a real construction problem.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: Section 13.3(c), by contrast, has the parties 'covenant and agree' to include apportioned amounts in their budgets (subject to their budget processes), so the compact is inconsistent about whether funding commitments bind. The 2014 WRDA endnote shows Congress had to legislate an allocation duty.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: 'Notwithstanding any other provision of this compact' is an express override and the mechanics (private placement, optional guaranty) are clear. Low.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: It overrides 12.13's mandatory competitive sale and sits against 12.3's bar on imposing bond obligations on signatory parties, though the guaranty is voluntary and constitutionally conditioned. The override is deliberate but broad.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: A plain enabling provision for receipt of funds in any form. Low.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: Duplicates 3.6(g), 14.1(a)(2) and 14.13(a); redundancy without conflict, though 15.1(e) reserves federal budgetary control. Low.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: 'All public and private projects and facilities which are required, in the judgment of the commission, for the optimum planning, development... of the water resources' makes the commission the judge of what 'optimum' requires, and the mandatory proviso about court decrees is a different kind of requirement bolted on. 'Optimum' and 'required' are both nameable open terms.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: The comprehensive plan is the yardstick for Section 3.8 approval, for 11.1(b) and 11.2(b) expenditure bars, and for 5.2 and 10.5 standards, yet 15.1(s) lets the President suspend, modify or delete plan provisions — so the measure against which private projects are judged is unilaterally alterable. That interaction is a live construction problem.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: 'During the ensuing six years or such other reasonably foreseeable period as the commission may determine' fixes a number and then dissolves it in the same breath, so the six-year figure has no binding force. That self-undoing quality is a nameable defect.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: Section 3.2(b) describes the same programme with only the 'reasonably foreseeable period' formula and no six-year default, so the two statements of one duty differ. Minor but specific.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: A one-line content requirement; nothing to construe.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: Tracks 3.2(b)'s wording. Low.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: 'Including all public and private projects to be anticipated' is broad and undefined but is a listing requirement, not a regulatory trigger. Modest.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: It sweeps in 'all public and private projects' whereas 3.8 reaches only those of 'substantial effect' — the same threshold mismatch that runs through 3.2(b) and 11.2(b). Named and real, though the consequence here is only informational.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: A short, definite requirement for a separate statement. Nothing.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: Mirrors 3.2(b)'s closing clause. Low.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: A concrete annual capital budget requirement with specified contents. Low.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: Consistent with 3.2(c) and 14.4(b)'s hearing requirement. Low.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: Detailed budget mechanics, but the apportionment rule — the balance 'shall be apportioned equitably among the signatory parties by unanimous vote' — combines an undefined standard ('equitably') with a unanimity requirement that gives every party a veto over its own share. That combination is a genuine construction and deadlock problem.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: Section 2.5 sets majority voting as the default and this requires unanimity; 13.3(c)'s covenant to fund is itself subject to each party's budget process; and 15.1(e) reserves federal appropriation control, which is why WRDA 2007 and 2014 had to direct the Secretary to allocate funds. The endnote documents that the funding chain did not work as written.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: 'Covenant and agree to include the amounts so apportioned... subject to such review and approval as may be required by their respective budgetary processes' promises payment and then makes it contingent on the promisor's own discretion — the covenant may be illusory. A named, classic defect.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: It sits against 12.20(a), which disclaims any mandatory funding obligation, and against 15.1(e)'s reservation of federal appropriation authority; the WRDA endnotes show Congress legislating to force allocation, confirming the covenant did not bind. Specific and documented.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: A bare stem introducing auxiliary powers. Nothing.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: Leads a list that overlaps 3.6 and 12.20(c); redundancy only. Low.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: 'Enter intro contracts' is a plain typographical error for 'enter into contracts'; it is obvious and self-correcting, so it does not change meaning, but it is a mechanical mistake on the face of the text. 'Sue and be sued in all courts of competent jurisdiction' is otherwise clear.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: New York § 634 supplies a special definition of 'court of competent jurisdiction' precisely for this sub-item, and 15.1(p) grants original federal jurisdiction while reserving United States immunity — so who may sue this body, and where, is addressed in three places. Moderate.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: A long enumeration of receivable items closing with 'and other funds, properties and services' — a catch-all after specifics, though nothing coercive turns on it. Modest.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: Duplicates 3.6(g), 12.20(c) and 14.13(a) with slightly different wording each time; 15.1(e) reserves federal budget control. Redundancy, not conflict.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: A concrete planning-and-specifications power. Nothing to construe.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: Overlaps 3.9(c) and 3.6(a). Low.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: 'Control and regulate the use of facilities owned or operated by the commission' is narrow and definite. Low.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: Consistent with 3.7's rate-setting over the same facilities. Low.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: A long verb-and-means string ending in 'or otherwise as it may deem necessary', a catch-all closing an enumerated list of acquisition methods. Modest.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: It permits sale and conveyance of property while 12.18 makes pledged revenues and 12.6 the disposition of facilities subject to indenture restrictions, and 14.14/14.15 govern acquisition from public bodies. Coordinated.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: 'All corporate powers essential to the declared objects and purposes of the commission' is a pure catch-all at the end of an enumerated list — the classic general-versus-specific structure, and 'essential' does no real limiting work. Nameable.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: It duplicates 3.6(h)'s implied-powers clause, so the compact contains two open-ended residual grants, each of which could be used to bypass the enumerated limits in Articles 4 through 11 and the reservations in 15.1. That doubling is what makes the residual grants contestable.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: A bare stem, 'subject to the provisions of this compact'. Nothing.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: Distinguishes commissioner functions from commission powers in (a); consistent with 2.5 and 14.5. Low.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: 'Except as otherwise provided by or pursuant to this compact' is a broad but conventional saving. Low.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: The phrase 'or pursuant to' lets commission rules under 14.2 reallocate the commissioners' own governing powers, a small circularity with 14.5(a)'s delegation to the executive director. Minor.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: 'Subject to any provisions of law specifically applicable to agencies or instrumentalities created by compact' points to an unidentified and possibly empty body of law. That indeterminate referent is a nameable softness.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: It intersects 15.1(m)'s direction that the commission is not a federal agency for specified statutes and 15.1(n)'s denial of federal-employee status — the compact does not otherwise say what law governs it. Moderate.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: A short internal-organisation duty. Nothing.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: Overlaps 2.6's self-organisation power; harmless duplication. Low.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: 'Appoint the principal officers' leaves 'principal' undefined. Small.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: Section 14.5(a) says the commission appoints only the executive director and that 'all other officers and employees shall be appointed by the executive director' — which conflicts with a commissioner duty to appoint 'the principal officers'. That is a specific, nameable inconsistency.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: A broad personnel power qualified by 'subject to the provisions of this article'; concrete in subject matter. Low-moderate.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: It is limited by 14.5(b)'s merit rule and 14.8's disqualifications, and it overlaps 14.5(a)'s allocation of appointment power to the executive director. Same tension as at 14.1(b)(4).

judgments.reasoning_cat1: A four-word contracting power. Nothing.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: Constrained by 14.9's bidding rules and 14.8(c)'s voiding of tainted contracts. Consistent.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: A bare stem. Nothing.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: Introduces rulemaking and peace-officer powers; no conflict at the stem. Low.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: The exemption from hearing and filing for rules 'which deal[] solely with the internal management of the commission' turns on the undefined word 'solely' and on where internal management ends — a nameable boundary problem in a provision that determines whether a rule is effective at all.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: Rules made here are enforceable by penalty under 14.17 and are the vehicle for 3.8's project-review procedure and 10.3's quantity thresholds, so whether a rule was validly adopted has instrument-wide consequences. The filing requirement also depends on five different states' administrative-procedure laws.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: 'Vested with the powers of a peace officer of the state in which he is duly assigned' is a sweeping grant achieved by designation alone, with no limit tied to compact business. The breadth is striking but the words are clear.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: It confers state police powers on commission employees who, under 15.1(n), are not federal officers and whose commission is, under 15.1(m), not a federal agency — the status question is unresolved instrument-wide. Moderate.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: The in-lieu payment formula — 'annual amounts which shall equal the taxes lawfully assessed upon property for the tax year next prior to its acquisition by the commission for a period of ten years' — is syntactically ambiguous as to whether 'for a period of ten years' modifies the payments or the assessment, and 'the payments may be thereupon terminated or continued in such reasonable amount as may be necessary or desirable' gives no standard at all. Both are nameable.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: It exempts the commission from taxation 'by or under authority of any of the signatory parties', which by 1.2(h) includes the United States, while 11.3 reserves state taxing power over withdrawals and 11.4(d)(ii) separately provides for apportioning in-lieu payments. Overlapping and partly duplicative regimes.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: 'All meetings of the commission shall be open to the public' is absolute and unqualified — no executive session, no exception for personnel or litigation. Its very absoluteness is what would be litigated.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: It admits no exception even for the personnel actions contemplated by 14.5, 14.8(b) and 14.11(d), or for bond negotiations under 12.13 — so read literally it is hard to reconcile with the rest of Article 14. That is a genuine whole-instrument strain.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: An enumerated list of hearing occasions closing with the general 'and in all other cases wherein this compact requires a public hearing', which is a cross-reference rather than a catch-all; notice requirements are specific. Low-moderate.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: The catch-all sweeps in 3.7, 4.4, 5.2, 6.2(b), 8.4, 9.4, 10.2 and 10.4, and 6.2(b) points back here for its manner of hearing — a coherent hub. But 4.4 requires a hearing on 'each proposed project' while 3.8 requires none, a gap this section does not close.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: A short public-records rule limited to minutes. Definite.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: Narrower than 14.4(a)'s open-meetings rule and 14.11(a)'s public distribution of audits; consistent. Low.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: 'A majority of the full membership' is precise, and the allocation of appointment power is stated in flat terms. The only softness is 'such additional officers, deputies and assistants as the commission may determine'.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: It gives the executive director power to appoint 'all other officers and employees', which contradicts 14.1(b)(4)'s direction that the commissioners 'appoint the principal officers of the commission'. That is a specific, nameable conflict between two operative provisions.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: 'No political, racial, religious or residence test' is a closed list and 'solely on the basis of merit and fitness' is a familiar civil-service standard; the mandatory removal sentence is unusually absolute but clear.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: The mandatory removal here sits alongside 14.8(b)'s forfeiture for wilful violations and 14.11(d)'s forfeiture for refusing audit assistance — three separate removal regimes with different triggers and no stated procedure. Moderate.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: A definite fifteen-day oath requirement. Nothing.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: It covers the executive director and officers appointed by him, but not commissioners, whose oath obligations arise elsewhere; a gap rather than a conflict. Low.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: 'Each officer shall give such bond and in such form and amount as the commission may require' is entirely discretionary but unambiguous. Low.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: The word 'bond' here is used in a wholly different sense from Article 12's debt instruments, an unflagged homonym within one instrument. Minor but real.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: A bare stem introducing three prohibitions. Nothing.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: Applies to 'commissioner, officer or employee' while (b)'s forfeiture reaches only 'officer or employee' — the mismatch is created here and in (b). Moderate-low.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: 'Financially interested, either directly or indirectly' has no de minimis threshold and 'indirectly' is undefined — a genuinely broad prohibition whose boundary would matter to anyone holding, say, shares in a contractor. Nameable.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: The commissioners are the Governors of four states ex officio under 2.2, so a strict reading of 'indirectly... in any contract... to which the commission is a party' is difficult to apply to sitting Governors whose states contract with the commission under 3.9(b) and 14.13. That is a real whole-instrument problem.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: 'Money or any other thing of value' with a carve-out for compensation and expenses paid by the commission; the phrase 'within the scope of his official duties' is a familiar limit. Low-moderate.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: Section 15.1(r) permits the United States to pay compensation to the federal member and advisor, and 2.4 says members serve without compensation — so payments from a signatory party sit awkwardly against a flat bar on accepting value 'in addition to the compensation... paid him by the commission'. Nameable.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: A narrow anti-bribery prohibition; definite. Low.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: Consistent with 14.5(b)'s merit rule. Low.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: 'Any officer or employee who shall willfully violate' with automatic forfeiture is definite, but 'willfully' adds a mental element absent from (a)'s prohibitions and the sanction omits commissioners entirely. That mismatch is visible on the face of the text.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: Paragraph (a) binds 'commissioner, officer or employee' but (b) sanctions only officers and employees — and commissioners are Governors, whom the commission plainly cannot remove. The gap between prohibition and sanction is specific and unresolved elsewhere.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: 'Knowingly made in contravention of this section is void' — 'knowingly' by whom is unstated, which matters a great deal to an innocent counterparty. A short provision with a nameable ambiguity.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: Voiding contracts collides with 14.1(a)(1) and (b)(6)'s contracting powers and with 12.6's assurance that bondholders 'ha[ve] recourse to all of the provisions... and [are] bound thereby' — a third party's rights under a void contract are not addressed. Moderate.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: A saving clause preserving other criminal and civil sanctions; clear. Low.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: It applies federal law and the law of the state 'in which such misconduct occurs', which parallels 14.17's penal sanction structure and 15.1(m)-(n)'s status provisions. Consistent.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: Two different dollar thresholds, a 'lowest responsible bidder' standard, a negotiated-purchase escape after rejection, and a waiver stem — 'responsible' is undefined and the negotiated-purchase route substantially undercuts the bidding requirement it follows. The interplay between mandatory bidding and the open-market fallback is genuinely contestable.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: The 1961 dollar thresholds have never been indexed and 15.1(j) subjects contracts over $10,000 to Walsh-Healey while 15.1(i) imposes Davis-Bacon on construction — three overlapping procurement regimes with different triggers. Moderate.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: A specific waiver ground for governmental purchases; definite. Low.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: Consistent with 3.9(b)'s power to employ signatory agencies. Low.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: 'The public exigency requires the immediate delivery' is a classic elastic emergency standard with no declaration procedure and no time limit. Nameable, though a common formula.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: Unlike 3.3(a) and 10.4, which require formal findings and hearings for emergencies, this waiver requires none — an inconsistency in how the compact treats exigency. Modest.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: 'Only one source of supply is available' is short and factual, though 'available' admits of argument in any sole-source dispute. Low-moderate.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: Nothing else in the compact addresses sole-source procurement. Low.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: 'Of a technical nature' and 'necessary in order to assure standardization... in the public interest' stack three open standards in one waiver ground. Nameable vagueness.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: No competing provision governs standardisation purchases. Low.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: 'Services... of a specialized or professional nature' is undefined and is the broadest of the five waiver grounds; it closes an enumerated list and could swallow much of the bidding requirement. A genuine list-scope problem.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: It coexists with 14.11(a)'s selection of accountants and 9.4's negotiated development contracts, both of which assume non-competitive engagement of professionals. Consistent.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: 'Against loss of revenue from any cause whatsoever' is an unbounded catch-all closing a list of insurable risks, though it merely authorises purchase rather than imposing liability. Modest.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: The coverage is made 'subject to the requirements of any agreement arising out of the issuance of bonds', tying it to 12.6 and 12.18; consistent. Low.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: 'As soon as practical after the closing of the fiscal year' sets no deadline and 'accepted accounting practices' is a soft standard, but the independence and distribution requirements are concrete. Modest.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: It coexists with 14.11(b)'s signatory audits, (c)'s GAO audit and New York § 640's comptroller examination — four audit regimes over the same books. Overlapping but not contradictory.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: 'All of the books, documents, records, files and accounts and all other papers, things or property' is a very broad enumeration closing with a sweeping residual, and 'at any time' has no limit. The breadth is nameable but the intent is plain.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: New York § 640 invokes this paragraph to authorise its comptroller, and 15.1(q) reserves congressional information demands — layered but consistent. Low-moderate.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: 'The general accounting office' and 'the comptroller general of the United States' are identified precisely; 'principles and procedures applicable to commercial corporate transactions' is unusual but specific enough. Low.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: It subjects the commission to GAO audit while 15.1(m) says the commission 'shall not be considered a Federal agency' for a list of federal statutes — the two characterisations pull in different directions, though 15.1(m)'s list is closed. Moderate.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: 'Refuse to give all require assistance' is a plain grammatical error for 'all required assistance', and 'shall forfeit his office' is an automatic sanction with no procedure. The error is obvious but the sanction's automatic quality is the more consequential defect.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: It creates a third automatic-forfeiture trigger alongside 14.5(b) and 14.8(b), each with different wording and none with a stated procedure. That inconsistency across Article 14 is nameable.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: A plain annual reporting duty plus a discretionary publication power. Nothing to construe.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: Overlaps 3.6(f)'s publication power and 15.1(q)'s congressional information right. Low.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: A bare stem. Nothing.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: Introduces powers that duplicate 12.20(c) and 14.1(a)(2). Low.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: 'Preliminary expenses such as the expenses incurred in the making of borings, and other studies of subsurface conditions' uses 'such as' to introduce examples, leaving the class of preliminary expenses open. A modest ejusdem generis point.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: Sits alongside 12.2's very broad definition of fundable purposes and 12.20(c); overlapping authorisations. Low-moderate.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: 'Either as grants or loans' with 'necessary or convenient' as the standard; permissive and clear enough. Low.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: Repayment terms are supplied by 14.13(b), and 12.20(a) disclaims any mandatory obligation to provide funds. Consistent.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: 'Payments... for benefits received or to be received' — 'benefits' is unquantified, echoing 4.3's assessment problem, but this is a permissive authorisation rather than a charge. Modest.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: It parallels 4.3's benefit-based assessments and 11.4's cost-sharing formulas without a stated relationship among them. Moderate-low.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: 'Shall be repaid... through the issuance of bonds or out of other income' with terms 'as may be agreed upon' — a mandatory repayment whose terms are left entirely to later agreement. That is a nameable indefiniteness.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: It commands repayment while 12.18 makes pledged revenues a trust fund unavailable for other purposes and 12.1 makes bonds payable solely out of commission revenues — so the repayment source may be encumbered. Moderate.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: 'This grant of power of eminent domain includes but is not limited to' expressly opens the enumeration, and the double exclusion ('other than property of a signatory party and any property held... in connection with a diversion authorized by a United States Supreme Court decree') is syntactically ambiguous as to whether 'other than' governs both limbs. That is a real reading problem in a condemnation power.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: The decree carve-out tracks 3.5(a) and (c), and the public-utility proviso preserves state regulatory authority consistent with 1.5 — coordinated. But the exclusion of 'property of a signatory party' sits against 14.15(a)-(b), which contemplate voluntary conveyance by those same parties.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: A clean two-tier choice-of-law rule for condemnation procedure with a stated default. Low.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: Consistent with 15.1(m)'s statement that the commission is not a federal agency for certain purposes, which bears on which 'federal law applicable to the commission' exists. Moderate-low.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: A flat allocation of the award to the commission and an equally flat immunity for the signatory parties. Definite.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: It bars liability of signatory parties consistent with 12.3, but 12.1's limitation of the commission's obligations to its own revenues means a condemnee's award may exceed available funds. A latent gap rather than a conflict.
